title: Ang 527–536: Devgandhari
tomorrow: why would a Guru call the world's love false?

segments.voice: Last time, five Bhagats closed Gujri, and Ravidas, finding every gift already used, offered body and mind. A new raga now, and a new question.

It's dusk in a neighborhood you don't know. Your phone's nearly dead, the map keeps spinning, and the house you need is down one of these lanes. So you do the old thing. You ask. An aunty watering her plants points left. A kid on a bike says, follow me. And you do, a little behind, trusting someone who knows the way. On ang 527, Guru Ram Das is standing at that same corner, asking that same question, about someone he loves.
screen: `LOST AT DUSK.` → `YOU ASK.` → `FOLLOW ME.` → `THE SAME CORNER, ANG 527.`

segments.voice: Devgandhari opens with his question. In paraphrase: tell me, in which lane, which gali, will I meet my Beautiful One? You saints of the Lord, show me the path, and I'll follow behind. The Beautiful One is the Lord. The Gurus often speak this way, as a bride longing for her beloved, and here she's out in the streets, asking. Notice how she asks. No demand, no map of her own, no pride about finding it alone. She stops the ones who know the way and walks behind them. Then, in paraphrase again: the Beloved's words are sweet to my heart; this is the good way to walk. So that's the answer to the corner. The lane isn't marked on any map. It's the one the Lord's people are already walking, and you find it by asking them and following. The outline calls Devgandhari a short, gentle raga, and you can hear why in this first hymn. The longing is real, but the voice stays soft. It asks. It follows. It's gentle.
screen: `WHICH LANE TO THE BEAUTIFUL ONE?` · `ASK THE ONES WHO KNOW.` · `FOLLOW BEHIND.` · `A SOFT VOICE, A REAL LONGING.` · then, large: `GENTLE.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly for the first part of the sit: a few steps across the room and back, unhurried, as if following someone down a lane. Then sit for the rest, and let the pace stay that slow inside. You can read the opening hymn on ang 527 first.
Ang 527. Where Devgandhari begins, with Guru Ram Das asking which lane leads to the Beautiful One.
Gentle: ask the way, then follow behind the ones who know it. Day fifteen-oh-six, one lane at a time.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading the Granth in order reach Devgandhari after Gujri; its hymns are sung in kirtan, and the bride asking the way to her Beloved is a common image in the Gurus' hymns.

pairs: where to meet the Beautiful One

myth: Sikh teaching says you must find the way to God all on your own
Guru Ram Das asks the Lord's saints for the path and follows behind.
Devgandhari begins with a question about which lane to take
tell me, in which lane will I meet my Beautiful One?
'my Beautiful One' in this hymn means a human sweetheart
the Beautiful One is the Lord; the bride's love-language is how the Gurus speak of longing for God.

fork.setup: first week at a new job. you could ask the senior nurse how she does the chart, or quietly figure it out alone to look capable. what fits ang 527?
options: ask her, and follow the way of the one who knows.
figure it out alone; asking makes you look weak.

fork.reveal: the bride doesn't pretend to know the lane. she asks the ones who walk it and follows behind. gentle, and it works.

original.note: Gurmukhi: gali, a lane or street; 'kit gali', in which lane (ang 527).

what a scholar hears: mero sundar kahahu milai kit gali, ang 527; a bride's question, asked softly, which fits how the outline hears Devgandhari.
